utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. All the accused are here. The Prosecution, I notice Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Mitchell. Defence, I notice the absence of Mr. Ostojic, Ms. Nikolic, and that's it. Good morning to you, Mr. Jevdjevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, I understand that you haven't finished your cross-examination after all. You need another 15 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Indeed, 15 minutes. And that would be to finish this morning and to clarify the issues I raised last Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine. Any remarks, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. And you, Mr. Petrusic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Bourgon, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Jevdjevic.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Further to my cross-examination of last Friday, there are a few questions which I would like to put to you to clarify one issue which was raised concerning the appointment of General Krstic as commander of the Drina Corps. I would like to begin by showing you a document I referred to last Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I can have in e-court 4D124, please. Sir, this document that will appear before you, you had the opportunity to read it last Friday, and I suggested to you during my cross-examination that you had seen this document when preparing for your testimony in the Krstic case. Now, having verified the matter, further to the objection that was raised by my colleagues, I know that this is not the document that you saw, because I read the transcript over again in the Krstic case.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but I'm not receiving the interpretation, and I haven't been since this session began.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You should have told us straight away. I'm not in a position to know, because I'm not following in Serbo-Croat. Let me, with your indulgence, go -- are you receiving interpretation now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm going to read out what was stated, Mr. Bourgon's question. He said following -- he showed you document 4D124, which you should have in front of you, and he told you: "Sir, this document that will appear before you, you had the opportunity to read it last Friday, and I suggested to you during my cross-examination that you had seen this document when preparing for your testimony in the Krstic case. Now, having verified the matter -- having verified the matter further to the objection that was raised by my colleagues, I know that this is not the document that you saw, because I read the transcript over again in the Krstic case." And then you told us that you were not receiving interpretation. From now on, I will leave you again in the hands of Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So, sir, the only thing I would like to confirm with you this morning is: Having read the transcript in the Krstic case over again, where you stated, at page 7104, that in preparing for your testimony then, you read the order of the president of the Republika Srpska, dated 13th of July, appointing General Krstic, so I would just like to confirm that the document that you saw then was the actual order signed by President Karadzic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, having confirmed this, I would like to move to document 7DP1032. If I can have this document in e-court, please. If I can have page 3 in English and page 2 in B/C/S. Sir, this is the document that I referred to on Friday, and it's a document, as you can see, which is signed by General Zivanovic in his capacity as corps commander, and I take it you see that the timing of this document or the signing of the document was 1600 hours on 13 July.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Could counsel please verify exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So that's the document, sir, I referred to last Friday, and can you tell me what you see in the signature block of this document, and if you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If we go back to the first page of the document, please, my first question relates to the addressees of this order. Can you confirm, on the basis of what is at the top of the document, that this document is, in fact, an order which would have been sent to all subordinate units of the Drina Corps, including, of course, the Bratunac Brigade and the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And also that this order, originating from the Drina Corps Command, was also sent to the Drina Corps Forward Command Post?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you recall receiving this document at the Drina Corps Forward Command Post in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. Possibly, it did arrive, but I personally don't remember this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, if I look at this document, and you have most of the document before you, and we can look also at the second page, can you confirm that this order was drafted in accordance with the standing operating procedures applicable within the VRS and the Drina Corps, that the format of the order is standard?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if I look at the second paragraph of this document, you will agree with me that as a result of this order, all addressees are provided with information concerning the Muslim forces heading for Tuzla, going through Crni Vrh and Cerska; is that, General, what it says in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if I go down to paragraph 1 of the order, which you have -- I think we need to go back one page back in the English document, but you have it in B/C/S. Can you confirm that by this order, the brigade commands are told to take all practical measures to discover, to block, disarm, and capture Muslim groups who are attempting to join their territory?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if you look at paragraph 3 of this order, would you agree with me that the order issued to all brigades is to put captured and disarmed Muslims into suitable buildings? So there is an order to secure the prisoners, and I would like to know what your understanding is by "buildings that can be secured by small forces."

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that the person issuing the order and drafting this order bore in mind the fact that the bulk of the forces of the Drina Corps was engaged in combat in different areas up at the front, combat operations in the Krivaja Operation and Stupcanica 95 and that there were very few available soldiers to deal with military security of the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that would be the reason why they are told to find suitable buildings which will require little manpower to secure the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. In my opinion, that would be it, exclusively.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if I move to paragraph 7 of the document - I need to go to the next page, please - I'd like you to read paragraph 7, and tell me if you agree that as a result of this paragraph, brigades would see it necessary to increase or to improve the level of radio communications discipline.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was an ongoing task.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And following the reception of such an order, officers would make an effort to increase radio discipline; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would be logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'd like to move to a further document, which will be the last one, which is 4D81. I would like first to go to the last page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, this is also a document I referred to during our cross-examination on Friday. Can you tell me, according to the signature block and the stamp, your understanding as to who sent this document and to whom it was received by?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can see here, what I've been shown on my screen, shows that the document was sent by the commander, Major General Radislav Krstic, and I see his signature there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in what capacity is General Krstic signing?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He signed this in the capacity of commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And according to the stamp, when was this document sent and received, if you can tell by the information that is provided to you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a document signed and typed out in this way was received in the centre of communications at 1945 hours, the encryption station, and the coder managed to process it, encode it, at 2010 hours, and then handed over -- and then this was handed over to all the subordinate units to whom it was intended, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can go to the first page of the document, I would like you to confirm first that this a regular combat report, and of course this is what it says on the document, but can you tell me who would have prepared this document and to whom it was sent, according to the information on the first page?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document was compiled by the Drina Corps Command, and this regular combat report was sent to the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So would I be right that this document includes, in some form, an overview of the information which was obtained from the combat reports submitted by all subordinate units of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should contain information of all the Drina Corps units which arrived at the Command of the Drina Corps on that particular day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I just have one slight translation issue. At one point, this document, which as we've just heard, was sent to the Main Staff, it got translated as "handed over," which sounds like handed to somebody. If that could be cleared up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, thank you, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's page 7, line 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I thank my colleague for this observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So page 7, line 8, sir, if I can draw your attention, the way your answer was translated was that the document was handed over. Was the document handed over or transmitted to all subordinate units to which it was intended?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In military terminology, a telegraph is either received or "predati," transmitted or -- I see no actual difference between "handed over" or "sent out," but what it implies is through the communications system, the telegram was sent out.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, sir, if you look at this document and what you've seen of it today, would you agree that this report could not have been sent without General Krstic being informed of its content?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if we look at paragraph 3 of the document, which you have on your screen, if we can just raise the document a little bit, is it your understanding of this paragraph that Muslim civilians -- that the fact that Muslim civilians and soldiers were being detained in Konjevic Polje and Nova Kasaba, that this is information that was in the possession of the Drina Corps Command before sending this report?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. I won't need this document anymore. I only have two further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The first one relates to something that we discussed when I met you last week, and I'd like you to confirm, and this is something also that was discussed in your interview with the Prosecution, that you agree there existed in 1995 in the VRS a culture of always covering your actions by the production of a written document.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And a good example of this, to show what we mean by a culture of always producing a written document, would be that when General Krstic decided to send back the commander of the Zvornik Brigade, Pandurevic, back to Zvornik, along with his tactical group, that this was an important decision, it was something that could have an impact on the Zepa operations, and then we saw last week that General Krstic immediately followed up with a written order. Would that be a good example of a culture of always producing a written document?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one can understand it that way. I think that the document was compiled by someone in the Drina Corps Command in Vlasenica and dispatched it to the Zvornik Brigade as timely information that in the area of responsibility, because of the newly arisen problems, Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic was covering back with his unit from Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, that was the reason of the document, but my question is: The production of the document is to, in fact, make official and to cover the decision of General Krstic to send back Colonel Pandurevic to the Zvornik area?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, you could consider it to be that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And my last question is the following: I'd just like to confirm, this is something that came from your interview in the -- sorry, your testimony in the Krstic case, that when you prepared for your testimony in that case, you spoke with Major Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I talked to him specifically more about the situation -- about situations which were informal, because the two of us were in totally different areas of the Drina Corps, so the information that one of us had with respect to the situation and his surroundings, the other didn't, because we were in completely different areas and dealt with completely different assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. I have no further questions. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: We decided not to cross-examine this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lazarevic. Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I will cross-examine this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and Mr. Jevdjevic, good morning. My name is Dragan Krgovic. I appear for General Gvero, and on his behalf I will be asking you questions connected with your testimony up to now. Mr. Jevdjevic, in your testimony so far, you spoke about the time you spent at Pribicevac, and my question is the following: At that Forward Command Post, you were able to send combat reports directly either to the Main Staff or to the Command of the Drina Corps; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were able to send reports directly to the Command of the Drina Corps. But as for the Main Staff, we sent telegrams to them through the mediation of the Command of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: My colleague, Mr. Petrusic, showed you a document which was one of the reports sent to the Main Staff. Could the witness be shown 6D22, please. Mr. Jevdjevic, this is one of those reports. Answering a question put to you by my learned friend Mr. Petrusic, who asked you about paragraph 4 of this report, you confirmed that you were aware of the event described in this combat report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In item 2 of this report, it also says that on that day, the 9th of July, as you testified before this Court, the operation concerning the enclaves was practically concluded on that day?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And practically on that day, there was no combat, except for fortifying the strengthening the positions reached by the brigade in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the 9th of July, yes. On the 9th of July, there was combat. The units of the Zvornik Brigade took Zivkovo Brdo on that day, and they spent the night at the positions they had reached.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But when answering my friend's question, you said that they completed fortifying the positions at around 1800 hours and that another unit arrived to take up those positions, and they withdrew to take a rest?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the evening, usually --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic and Mr. Krgovic, both of you, please, slow down, because you are overlapping. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Usually, in the evening positions would be fortified, and sometimes when the situation allowed, those units that had been carrying out assault actions on that day would hand over the lines they had reached to the reserve units accompanying them or following them, and they would withdraw to a suitable area where they could rest. Probably they would leave only some of their men behind to guarantee that the points reached during the night would be protected, and they would withdraw some of the units to suitable areas to take a rest. That's what I said before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And the combat report that was sent reflects correctly the situation on the ground as you saw it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown Exhibit 6D328, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, this is a combat report also sent from the Pribicevac Forward Command Post, and it was sent on the 10th of July. It refers to the situation of UNPROFOR in the Srebrenica enclave. Please read this document, and I'm interested in paragraph 1, in which it says: "On the basis of surveillance and monitoring of the situation in the Srebrenica enclave, as well as the statements of UNPROFOR soldiers who surrendered to our forces and asked for our protection, we conclude that the Muslim army has surrounded UNPROFOR and assumed control over it. "The Muslims seized some of UNPROFOR's combat equipment (armoured combat vehicles, heavy artillery pieces and ammunition) and are using it in combat against our forces." Mr. Jevdjevic, my question is the following: Are you aware that such things occurred during the Srebrenica operation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps I was not careful enough during my preparation, but I really don't see where this document could come from. I don't see an ERN number. It's the first time I've seen it. I may have missed it, and if I did, I apologise to my colleague, but I would like to know where this document comes from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Are you in a position to enlighten us or at least enlighten your colleague?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I showed some of these documents to Mr. Simic. My investigator obtained them during his investigation, and I have the original available. I can show the original, if that would satisfy my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is hardly acceptable information. I mean what Mr. Petrusic is really interested in --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can tell you the source of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I just agree with Mr. Petrusic. We need the source.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, of course, and this is why I'm saying what you said doesn't help much. What we need to know is where your investigator got it from and if that -- it's a complete original.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when we wanted to introduce the statement of the late General Djukic, I asked his heirs for his notes and documents which might corroborate his statements, and that was how I obtained a certain number of documents. Some of those documents are on IDS and some are not. When the first document I used, which was the one I used with Novica Simic, was shown in the courtroom, I sent a circular e-mail to all my colleagues, explaining the source of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you satisfied with this, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, Your Honours. That mail was also sent to Mr. Petrusic's team, and I informed the Prosecutor orally a month ago that I would be using a number of documents which I obtained from that same source.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, thank you. Yes, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That first document was really sent, but not this one. This is really the first time I've seen it. To the best of my knowledge, the heir of General Djukic is supposed to come and testify here, so I hope we learn something more about this from him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrusic. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We have been in recent contact with the Gvero team and asking them about a document similar to this, and they refused to tell us where it was from, standing on what they felt was their right, so I'm not sure what counsel is referring to. If we can get the name of the heir, and I'm sure we can talk about this with counsel and sort it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. So let's proceed in the meantime and avoid wasting more court time. Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, please look at this document, does it roughly correspond or, rather, does it correspond to the information you had at Pribicevac at the time about the situation of UNPROFOR in the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this report reflects the information we had about UNPROFOR in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, to sum up some of the information you had available at the time on the 9th of July, you spoke about this in your testimony and it concerns the nature of the attack on the Muslim armed forces in the Srebrenica enclave, the information you had on that day, the 9th of July, was the following: That the attack by the army of Republika Srpska on the Muslim forces was being launched exclusively because the Muslims conducted incursions from the enclave and engaged in terrorist activities against both civilian and military targets; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That area had to be limited by military positions to prevent further circulation between the two enclaves, between Srebrenica, Kladanj, and Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You also had information that the civilian population was not the target of the attack by Republika Srpska; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You also had information that the UNPROFOR forces should not be targeted?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we had such orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You also had information that the Muslim forces attacked the UNPROFOR soldiers and that one of them had been killed?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You also had information that civilian targets should not be shelled, and neither should the town of Srebrenica itself; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And such reports were sent to the superior command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And whoever was able to read those reports had no reason to believe that the reports were untruthful; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that would be the only information that person would have, the information in the reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But to the best of your knowledge at the Forward Command Post of Pribicevac, this information corresponded to information on the ground, did it not?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, when testifying in the Krstic case, and that was on the 6th of November, 2000, on page 7068 you mentioned that at one point General Gvero briefly visited Pribicevac. Do you remember saying that when testifying in the Krstic case?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't mention the day on which this happened, but here before this Chamber you testified that this was on the 9th of July, 1995, at around noon, when General Gvero turned up at the Pribicevac Forward Command Post, stayed there for a brief period, and then left. Does this information correspond to what you saw at Pribicevac on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And on that day when General Gvero turned up, this was the information he was able to obtain at the Forward Command Post concerning the events in Operation Srebrenica; is that correct? I'm referring to my entire previous set of questions concerning combat reports and the situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, General Gvero stayed at the Forward Command Post for a short while, together with General Krstic. The information he received in writing was in good order. I don't know whether General Krstic might have told him about something else, but I was not with them while the two of them were together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you don't know what they talked about?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But this information that I asked you about was information available to General Krstic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, we'll move on to another topic now. I do apologise, Mr. Jevdjevic, for the pause. I'm looking at the transcript to avoid overlapping, as we speak the same language. In the course of your testimony, you mentioned that at one point in time, you went to Zepa, to the Forward Command Post of the Drina Corps in Zepa. My colleagues asked you in detail about the date, so I won't go into that again, but I'll just ask you this: In Zepa, did you have the same equipment that you had at the Pribicevac Forward Command Post?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, as I was able to understand your CV, you went to school in Rogatica. I assume that the Zepa-Rogatica area is familiar to you.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In July 1995, especially towards the end of July 1995, would you tell me, please, on the road from Rogatica to Boksanica, where there was an UNPROFOR check-point, were there any check-points manned by the army of Republika Srpska on the stretch of road from Rogatica to Boksanica, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I know is that there was a check-point at Boksanica. As for the rest of the road from Borike towards Rogatica, there was no reason for there to be a check-point, because that was in the depth of our territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And at Boksanica, it was an UNPROFOR check-point where negotiations were conducted with the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, can you tell me, how long does it take to go from Rogatica to Zepa along that road, under those conditions prevailing during the war, by car, by bus, or some other vehicle; how long does it take to get from Rogatica to Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About an hour and 15 minutes to an hour and a half, depending on which vehicle you used, but generally about an hour and a half, because there's a macadam road -- or was a macadam road halfway with serpentines and hairpin bends.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that at the end of July 1995, in that area of responsibility, that General Mladic arrived at Zepa and he spent some time there. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you also remember that during those days at the end of July, General Gvero tried to establish contact with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And General Mladic refused to speak to General Gvero; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that particular point, when General Gvero from the Main Staff rang up the Forward Command Post in the village of Godjeva [phoen] and asked to speak to General Mladic, General Mladic was not actually there at the time when the call came through, he wasn't at the Forward Command Post there, and I assume he was at Boksanica or elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did General Gvero tell you why he wanted to speak to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the conversation. The soldier who called up -- or, rather, answered the telephone gave the connection to me because General Mladic was not at the Forward Command Post, and on the other side there was General -- on the other side of the line there was General Gvero, and he asked me where General Mladic was, because he said he wanted to talk to him. And I told him that according to the information received, he was probably in the Boksanica region. And General Gvero then said that he needed to talk to him and to tell him of the seriousness of the situation during those days on the western front of Republika Srpska, to inform him of that. So I remember having that conversation with General Gvero.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And he said he was worried, did he, for the fate of the area, and that time was being lost, whereas the western part was falling; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those were roughly his comments, and I'm paraphrasing. He was very worried about the situation at the Krajina battle front, and the situation at Zepa at that point in time he considered to be satisfactory, militarily, with respect to the Republika Srpska forces. So he wanted to convey that information to General Mladic himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown Exhibit P1311 now, please. And in B/C/S, we'd like to have the page 1311C, and the English version, 1311A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This document is under seal, so there will be no broadcast of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In B/C/S, it's ERN 3205699 [as interpreted], and the English version, 0080165. 03205699. May I take a moment, Your Honour, because the witness can't actually see that page yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see that portion, Mr. Jevdjevic, right up at the top? It is a message for Panorama 1 to call Gvero urgently.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the frequency. I can't see the date. It was 0829 hours, as far as I can see here, a message for Panorama the 1st, call Gvero as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Panorama was the code name for the Main Staff, and Panorama the 1st was General Mladic; is that it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the jargon at the time, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The date is the 23rd of July, 1995, Your Honours. The 23rd of July. Mr. Jevdjevic, after this did General Gvero send a telegram of any kind addressed to General Mladic and the Forward Command Post?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember him sending it out the same day after my telephone conversation with General Gvero to the village of Godjenje and the Forward Command Post there. I think a telegram arrived from the Main Staff, and the encryptor, the soldier who did the encryption, received the telegram. And since General Mladic still wasn't at the Forward Command Post, he simply asked me what to do, because he had received a telegram from General Mladic and General Mladic was nowhere nearby. So he wasn't able to hand the telegram over to him. And as an encryptor, he had to dispatch the telegram, hand it over. And then I took the telegram myself purely to see what it was about, to see that it wasn't anything urgent. And in that case, if it were, I would take urgent measures to see that the telegram was handed over to General Mladic. And I saw that the telegram was to General Mladic personally, sent by General Gvero.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And the contents were similar to what he had told you when you talked to him over the phone, I mean General Gvero; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was roughly it. The contents were similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General Gvero asked that measures be taken to strengthen -- reinforce the front and to draw the commander's attention to that western part of the front; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all I remember is the telegram was written -- well, it was a high-sounding telegram, very well-chosen words, in which General Gvero personally addressed General Mladic and presented the full force of the situation, the difficulties facing the western front in Krajina, and quite simply, using a conciliatory tone, he was suggesting it would be a good idea that in this difficult situation that they were faced with, that the army of Republika Srpska was faced with, that it would be a good idea if he heard the opinions of his assistants and advisers, to hear their views on the situation, and that they should cooperate as they had been doing thus far. That's a rough paraphrase of the contents of the telegram. Because of the specific wording of the telegram, I happen to have remembered it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So General Gvero said discreetly to General Mladic that he shouldn't listen to his assistant and not to listen to the opinions of his assistants; was that the substance of the telegram, in actual fact?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a correction on page 21. The telegram was for Mladic, not to Mladic. That's an error in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Also, the last sentence in English just doesn't make much sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, there was an interpretation problem there. I asked you the question: General Gvero discreetly let General Mladic know, and he recommended that he listen to the suggestions of his helpers, assistants, and he was discreetly saying that he hadn't been doing that thus far, but he used a diplomatic tone?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how I understood those words. Well, they were nicely wrapped up, intellectually speaking, and he was sort of telling General Mladic, in a nice way, that faced with the situation as it was, that he should listen to the opinion of his assistants and the people around him. And what he wanted to say, that he wasn't paying due attention to what his assistants are telling him. So he's suggesting that because of the difficulties that he was facing at the front, the gravity of the situation at the front, they should cooperate as they had been doing before. That's how I understood the telegram.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And it had to do with the situation on the western front or the western part of the front?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Jevdjevic. I have no further questions for this witness, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krgovic. That concludes the cross-examinations from the Defence teams. Mr. McCloskey, roughly do you know how long you expect your cross to last? I'm not asking this in order to curtail your time, just to be able to organise ourselves better.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I will try to finish today, and it's hard to tell, but I'll try.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't want to go tomorrow. I can tell you that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Don't feel pressurised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, is it Colonel Jevdjevic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: My name is Peter McCloskey. I work for the Office of the Prosecutor. I'll be asking you some questions now. Just so I don't forget, let me kind of go back to where we left off. That day that General Gvero met with General Krstic at Pribicevac, where did they -- where did they meet; do you know? Was it at the observation post, or somewhere around the coms van, or where?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the Forward Command Post. It was a premises made up of earth. We didn't have any built facilities. But General Krstic at the time was at a small observation post from which you could just see the combat action going on from Zeleni Jadar towards Rina Bojna [phoen], so along those lines, and at that particular day he was at the observation post from which he could see those first combat actions undertaken by his units. And when General Gvero arrived, we greeted each other at the Forward Command Post there, and then he went some 50 metres further on, which is where General Krstic was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So General Gvero went out to the observation post with you to meet General Krstic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stayed by the device, and he went further on with his escorts. Whether there were two soldiers with him or a driver, they went on towards General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, your memory's been pretty amazing. Can you help us with how many people arrived with General Gvero?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think there were at least two people with him, whether the driver and someone else, but whenever a general was moving around, on his left and right there would be at least one of his escorts or officers, depending on who was with him in his environment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What kind of vehicle did he arrive in?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember what kind of vehicle it was, but he parked the vehicle at the entrance to the Forward Command Post, and I noticed him coming to those premises on foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm trying to ask as simple questions as possible, and if your answer can -- you can always explain an answer, but I'm just asking you the kind of vehicle and you added a whole lot extra, but -- which is okay, but we're going to be here for a while. Do you remember who else was out at that observation post with Generals Krstic and Gvero?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you remember where Mladic was that day that Gvero and Krstic were at the observation post?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did he come to Pribicevac that day; General Mladic, that is?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Mladic came the day after, was at Pribicevac the day after.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so your best recollection is that General Gvero came on what day?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my analysis and to the best of my recollections, he arrived on the 9th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And could we see Prosecution Exhibit 33.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, as we know, I think you'll agree with me that -- and I think we can tell from your testimony that the 9th was a very significant day for this operation, because as you have said, and I don't think it's contested among us, that the Operation Krivaja 95 was not meant to take the town of Srebrenica. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how I understood it, and that's how it was at the initial stages of that operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So then if you'll take a look at this document, which I know you've seen many, many times. This is the document addressed to Generals Gvero and Krstic personally, who you say were together at Pribicevac on the 9th, and you may recall this is the one that's from Tolimir. And this is the point where it says, in the second paragraph: "The president of the republic is satisfied with the results of combat operations around Srebrenica and has agreed with the continuation of the operation for the takeover of Srebrenica ..." So it's now -- this entire operation is now changed to actually go into the town of Srebrenica; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of what -- of the agreement given by the president of the Republika Srpska, the situation had changed. That was in the evening, at around midnight, of the 9th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, we see that that's when this document was received at the -- I'm not sure exactly. Can you tell where this document was received at?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was -- has been a correction here. It's not entirely clear, but I assume it was around 2350 hours or 2250 hours. I can't quite see it, whether it's a "2" or "3," I can't be quite precise. But, anyway, late at night of the 9th. Around midnight, a little before midnight perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, we see that there is a stamp on this, and I will recall, I think you said that -- can you make out this received stamp? You said there wasn't a stamp at the Pribicevac Forward Command Post, and this is addressed to the president as well as the Forward Command Post. So could this be the Presidency document?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very possibly. Well, I don't know if it's the Presidency document, but it wasn't received at the Forward Command Post, because we didn't have a stamp there, so it couldn't have been received there. And quite possibly this is a Presidency document, but it certainly wasn't at the Forward Command Post.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we go to the bottom of that document so we can show the witness and we can all see if there's anything down there. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But you do remember seeing a copy of this document at the Forward Command Post that night, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume a copy certainly got there, because it was an important telegram, but personally I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember the evening of the 9th, that the plan had changed and you're now going forward to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the telegram arrived, I assume we were all asleep, so I further assume that until -- that what this telegram deals with was realised on the 10th. It could have happened or arrived on the 10th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, it's also certainly possible that the copy of this document was received an hour or so before the Presidency received their document, just because sometimes it take a while to get the teleprinter going and working; correct? It could have been received after this one, too?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know what you mean, what you're referring to. I assume that this document could have arrived at the Forward Command Post -- well, it would be speculation. The Main Staff had direct communication with the Presidency, and up at the Forward Command Post the Main Staff went through the Drina Corps. But the work of these encoders and the speed at which communications were established are relative, so what you just said is quite possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And there's one particular part I want to draw your attention to. It says: "The president of the republic is satisfied with the results of the combat operations around Srebrenica and has agreed with the continuation of the operation." Now, when it says that the president has agreed, does that mean that General Mladic has made a proposal to the president to go on towards Srebrenica, and that the president agrees with that proposal? Under the normal functioning of the system, is that what we can infer from this document?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Theoretically speaking, the subordinate person gives the proposal to the superior, and the superior agrees or not. Now, whether this principle is applied to this document, I don't know, because we're dealing with the levels of Main Staff and Presidency, so it's a level far higher than me and further away from me. But that would be the general principle applied.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, you told us that you were hearing a lot of the discussions, and clearly information has travelled from the Forward Command Post to the decision-makers, to General Mladic probably, to the Drina Corps, to the Main Staff, and the decision-makers have made this decision clearly well before 2350 hours that evening; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible, but how much time beforehand, what information they had when, well, it was on the 9th, before nightfall, that we took those important features, Zivkovo Brdo and Alibegovac and arrived at the edges of the demilitarised zone, so that in the evening hours, after 2000 hours, up to 2300 hours, in the space of those three hours, the superior command could have been informed about the combat results of the Krivaja 95 operation. I absolutely allow for the possibility that within those two or three hours, both the Main Staff and the Presidency were informed of the course of the combat operations in the Krivaja 95 operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, Colonel. Anything's possible, but you were the hub of information coming from Pribicevac. No one had more information probably on this than General Krstic, who is, we know, a close colleague of yours. You were working with him that day. Do you recall any information going from the Forward Command Post relating to this important subject, "We are succeeding, we may be able to take advantage of the situation, we may be able to consider taking the next step," anything like that? This has major repercussions for you, it means the battle continues, it means a lot. So this is something you will remember, if you can remember anything?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This may sound incredible, but first of all not all information could go through me, because I was the officer in charge of establishing communication lines. I watched over them so as to make sure they were functioning without interruption. But this particular document certainly arrived at the Forward Command Post. That's quite logical. But believe me, I learned only recently that the president of the republic approved the extension of the attack towards Srebrenica. I did not know that it was the president of the republic who gave his approval. As I saw it, the situation on the front changed on the 10th of July, when I heard with my own ears the information that our units were being ordered to speedily take feature after feature and proceed towards Srebrenica. That I know very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, well, the foundation of most of your many, many hours of testimony was that you were in a position to be able to hear most of what was going on. But just to make it clear, you don't know anything about information coming out of the Forward Command Post to higher echelons regarding the decision to go forward?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My fundamental duty at the Corps Forward Command Post was to make sure communications were not interrupted from General Krstic to the commanders of the units participating in these two operations, and it was those communications that I constantly watched over, towards Trivic, Pandurevic, Blagojevic, and so on. This document arrived at the Forward Command Post, and when the cryptographer received it, he didn't give it to me because General Krstic is the addressee. He's not a colleague of mine but my commander. If General Krstic wasn't around, it was Colonel Vicic, his deputy, who would be handed the document. It was not necessary for me to read everything contained in the correspondence between the Forward Command Post and the Main Staff or the Presidency, nor was this in the rules. I know many of these communications because they refer directly to the situation, but there were others that I was not aware of, personally, and that I don't know about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you agree with me, when it comes to any information about the strategic move to take Srebrenica and information going to the higher echelons, you don't have any information about that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What higher echelons are you referring to? I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I can say it again. The Corps, the Main Staff, the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards communication with the Presidency, I knew absolutely nothing about it. Those were levels that were far above me, and it was well known who was in charge of communications with the Presidency and concerning what issues. The Main Staff was not carrying out those two operations, so we had very little communication with the Main Staff. I'm mostly aware of communications with the units participating in the Srebrenica and Krivaja operations and the sum of the general plan and general correspondence with the Corps Command. It was my duty to establish communications with the units and with the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you say it was well known who was in charge of establishing communication with the Presidency, so who was that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Main Staff, that's the first link in the chain of command that is connected to the Presidency. That's the logic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Of course, and you say it's well known, so who in the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the Main Staff was the number-one man communicating with the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And he was doing that, as far as you know, in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that, but I assume that it was he who was supposed to communicate with the Main Staff, just as I communicated to General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go back in time from Pribicevac now, and we'll come back to some of those issues a little bit later. I'm going to delve just a little bit into the radio relay communications that you spent so much time talking about. If we could go to 65 ter -- well, I'm just going to refer to this. I'm not going to go to it. There is a big complicated diagram, 65 ter 1D00322. It's the diagram used by Mr. Rodic. I think you talked about -- you saw the diagram that showed all the different connections with the radio routes and Veliki Zep and Vlasenica. It shows on this document that -- on page 15, that there is a numbered line from Vlasenica to Veliki Zep, and it's number 0674, according to what Mr. Rodic says. Do you remember any of those numbers or are you just kind of going along with what Mr. Rodic said?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no reason to doubt what Mr. Rodic says or to doubt this diagram.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, there it is. I tried to avoid it. In any event, if we look carefully, we'll see the section 0674 from Vlasenica to Veliki Zep. Do you know, could that be intercepted?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that in this triangle, it says "200." I don't know if you can help me, if you can see better than I can. Is it "200"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could, I guess -- no avoiding it. Can we bring it up? That square on the left side, if we could bring that up. Okay, that's what I'm talking about, "Veliki Zep," 0674 to Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had two relay directions from Vlasenica to Veliki Zep. One was encrypted and could not be intercepted. If it says "200" in that triangle which would be marking that particular device, then it could not be intercepted. If in the upper one it says "8," that's 0607, then theoretically that could be intercepted because they did not have an encryption device or a scrambling device.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter 2823. And the scrambling devices didn't always work, did they?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this radio relay direction, the devices protected, scrambled, or encrypted both oral and written communications. That was the kind of device it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But it didn't always work; right? It broke down sometimes?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This protected line between the Drina Corps and the Main Staff, I see in this telegram here 0674, had eight channels, and those were protected. And I don't remember that during the war that device, which protected both oral and written communications, broke down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's take a look at this document, and I want you to just look at the -- this is this 1993 list of frequencies that was used for the RRU-800, and it's got, for this number that we've been talking about, 0674, it's got "Frequency 859/762." And you've testified as far as you know that that wasn't changed throughout the entire war; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where do you see that, specifically?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Number 1.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards changing the frequencies, there's a long story behind that, which you probably --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, I don't want to hear the long stories. You talked about the long story. My first question is: As far as you know, that wasn't changed during the war; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From 1993 onwards, to the best of my knowledge, in the Drina Corps we did not change the frequencies of those radio relay devices, because we could have done that only if so ordered by the chief of communications of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But you're not sure? It's possible they were changed?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they had been changed, I would have known about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I see it's break time, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Twenty-five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, do you know a man from the -- he was in the -- I think it was the 67th Communications Unit from the Main Staff named Veljko Pajic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Velo Pajic, yes, I do know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You know he was working on these railway routes during the war, a pretty knowledgeable guy about them?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wasn't at the Veliki Zep node, but he is extremely knowledgeable concerning the routes in the -- the communications routes in the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, let me read to you. He testified here not long ago, I think November 26th, and was asked this question by my colleague and given this answer. It was the Prosecutor that asked him this question,

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: "The frequencies that were operating on the route that you described, 0607-0674, and the other routes you looked at in the document I showed you from 1993," by the way, that's the document on the screen - do you have a present recollection of what frequencies were operating in 1995?" And he said: "The frequency devices, RRU-800 and FM-200, we are talking about these two relay routes, 0607 and 0674. The range was between 610 to 960. Now, the transmission frequency, 783, on route 0674 in 1993, this applied in 1995. The transmission was 783, and that the -- the gap had to be 50 megahertz between emission and the reception." So in that question and answer, Mr. Pajic is saying that the frequency for 0674 was the frequency of 783; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have precise information as to what the frequencies were, because that would have been a vast amount of information for me. I don't know where he got this information. I never even knew precisely what frequencies we were working on. When we established communications, certain frequencies were taken up and they remained until there was some reason to change frequencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Again, a simple question, sir. He said that on 0674, the frequency was 783, and that was applicable for 1995. Do you have any reason to doubt his viewpoint on that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he would have to give you both the receiving and sending frequencies. There had to be two.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, you saw him say, "783." You don't have any doubt that he's correct about that, do you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, believe me, I don't doubt that he's right, just as I don't doubt this document that was sent by the chief of communications of the Main Staff, but -- well, if it was he, himself, who drew up this document or Velo Pajic, I don't know. All I know is that the frequencies never changed on this equipment unless there was a major reason to change them, because it was a lot of work. It was a huge procedure to change frequencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if there was a major reason, the frequencies could be changed?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there was a reason, yes, but that what would require many actions to be undertaken, much work to be done on the entire territory, because according to the technical rules, the range of these devices was 50 kilometres, and when there was optical visibility, the range was much longer, and you would have to get the approval of all the participants on the entire territory, even in other countries, using that frequency range. So you cannot change a frequency without it immediately affecting all the other participants and the entire network or grid, as it was called, of radio relay nodes and other owners of communication, such as television --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We've heard all about that from Mr. Pajic, but this is a very simple question. We can see from this document that this numbered route does not include frequency 783, so it's fair to conclude that either this document is wrong or they changed the frequency for 0674?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Mr. Pajic as a very hard-working, diligent and precise officer, so I have no reason now -- there's no way I can say whether it's he who is wrong or this document. Everything I say would be speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, if the VRS coms people suspected that the Muslims were able to intercept on a particular frequency, that would be a major reason that would be the cause to change frequencies, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be a reason, yes, but it would be insignificant, because the moment you escape from a certain frequency, whoever has intercepting equipment will find you in a minute on the next frequency, because his equipment scans the entire frequency range, just like when you're searching for a radio station on a transistor radio, you discover it in a moment. So we used other means to secure our lines. It was only if the enemy blocked our communication on a certain frequency that we would change frequencies, but he never did that, he never jammed our communications, because he wanted to listen in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's what he said. That's -- when the enemy testified, that's exactly what they said. But I can also tell you that it wasn't quite as easy as finding a radio station, according to the people that testified. But we won't go into that. Well, you've talked about some of the intercepts that -- where you remember the conversations, and those, I think, you probably recall from looking at the intercept yesterday, were captured from an RRU-1 set. And so I take it you had no contest that the Muslims were able to intercept the RRU-1 in certainly the conversations that you talked about yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a huge difference between an RRU-1 device and the RRU-800 and FM-200 devices. The aerial of the RRU-1 device has an angle of 60 degrees, and it's electromagnetic waves --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Believe me, we're -- if any of us were taking notes, we're experts at that, or we should be. My question was simple. We know there's a difference. Rodic didn't even challenge the RRU-1s. He just looked at the RRU-800s. And you didn't appear yesterday, when you were talking about the conversations you were involved in from certain frequencies on the RRU-1, you didn't appear to challenge their ability to intercept those conversations, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So we're okay on the RRU-1. RRU-800 is a little different matter; fair enough?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Would it surprise you -- when we go back and look at our intercepts, roughly 148 of them from the RRU-800 frequency range, the majority of those, I am told, come within the frequency 783. That was given to us by Mr. Pajic. Would that surprise you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would not surprise me, because I know there is a theoretical possibility for these conversations to be intercepted, because the spoken communication was not scrambled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Right. Okay, and going on to another subject, putting to bed the intercept subject, I hope, for now. Can you help, if you're in Zvornik or Bratunac and you're talking about the right bank of the Drina, what side -- what side of the Drina are you talking about? I mean, we know what the "left bank" means in Paris, but how about the right bank of the Drina?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Drina is a river flowing for most of its course in a south-north direction, and for most of its course it constitutes the border between present-day Serbia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. The right bank is to the east, and to the east of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that's where Serbia is. The left bank is to the west, so the West Bank of the Drina is part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the left bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So the right bank is Serbia; the left bank is Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for most of the course of the river, not throughout the whole course of the river.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, I think we've got a translation problem, because I know things were awfully messed up and confused, but I don't think the Drina was travelling in a north-south direction. That would be meaning it's going two different ways. What did you mean? Basically, northerly by Zvornik, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I wanted to say was that for most of its course, if you disregard its meandering, it flows from the south towards the north.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's what I thought. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the right bank of the River Drina, there is also Republika Srpska, Rudo, Cajnice, Visegrad. Those municipalities have a significant part of their territory on the right bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And we've heard over the years of the Birac region. Can you -- that's a large region, isn't it? Can you roughly describe this large Birac region, just very roughly and shortly? It's not a big deal.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Birac region implies a geographical area which stretches from the Romanija Plateau towards the Drina River. It's a hilly, mountainous area with small mountains, canyons and so on, and mostly the following municipalities are included: Vlasenica, Sehovici, Milici, Bratunac, Srebrenica, and I assume Zvornik in part. I'm not from that area, specifically, but I suppose part of the Zvornik municipality. So those are the municipalities which are purely geographically referred to as "Birac" and will be found on the map under "Birac."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, thanks, thank you. And I want to go to your testimony of yesterday [sic], and it's on page 29481, and it's when you were talking about the various operations you and General Pandurevic were involved in. You talk about one in particular, the spring of 1993, and you say: "In the spring of 1993, the Drina Corps was engaged in offensive activities on the area of Cerska, Konjevic Polje, Kasaba, and from the south towards Srebrenica, Osmaci, Zeleni Jadar and Pribicevac." Now, you were -- I believe you said you were in that operation with General Pandurevic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We weren't together. He took part from the Zvornik and Drinjaca axis, and the Forward Command Post of the Corps and I were within the framework of the combat units taking part from the Vlasenica direction. It was only on the wavelengths that we were together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There's an exhibit, and it's -- I can't remember the name of it or the number of it right now, but I just thought of it. It was a big map that was on the Zvornik Brigade, and it outlined various operations that Zvornik had been involved in during the war. And it mentions Cerska, Konjevic Polje, in 1993. It also mentions, as part of Cerska, Konjevic Polje, a couple of villages a little north of that, Kamenica and Liplje. Do you remember Kamenica and Liplje being part of that, too, or are those too small for you to remember?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember those specifically. What I do remember is Cerska, Konjevic Polje, Kasaba, and Kravica, so those locations, they're the ones I remember and they're the ones I took part in; in the liberation of those areas, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Right. And can you tell us what General Pandurevic -- I guess he was a colonel at the time, what his commander function for the overall operation was? Was he just the Zvornik Brigade, or was he overseeing the whole thing, or what?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His role was within the frameworks of the positions within his brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who was in overall command of that operation?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Milosevic, on behalf of the Corps Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And do you remember the name of the operation?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I think the operation went in stages and that it didn't have a specific name. Well, I don't remember the name, anyway, because it was done in stages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to 65 ter number 29. I'll just -- this is a -- I don't know if you've seen this before. Have you seen a document called "Directive 4," dated 19 November 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. I never saw any documents having the status of directives --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You knew that there were directives out there, though, didn't you? I mean, you would have received them over the teletype.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learnt when the proceedings started, the trial, but directives are documents which the Presidency of Republika Srpska sends to the Main Staff and its address.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, if we could go on page 11 in B/C/S, this talks about various areas, and I want to go to the Drina Corps now. The Drina Corps, on the 19th of November, I guess it had just formed. Hadn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Drina Corps was established on the 1st of November, but I can't read anything here, it's such a poor copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I can try to give you a hard copy, but -- it's a little bit better. And it's English page 5. And in this, the part I want you to take a look at starts with the Drina Corps. You'll see it there, all right, there near the top: "From its present positions, its main forces shall persistently defend Visegrad, the dam, Zvornik, and the quarter, while the rest of its forces in the wider Podrinje region shall exhaust the enemy, inflict the heaviest possible losses on him, and force him to leave the Birac, Zepa, and Gorazde areas, together with the Muslim population ...," and then it goes on. And if you look at the last page, well, I can tell you it's in the name of General Mladic and it was drafted by Major General Manojlo Milovanovic, the person you said was commanding the operation that you talked about Konjevic Polje and Cerska. Sir, do you know does this --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Sorry, that's a misstatement of the evidence. He said "General Milosevic."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry, I thought he said "Milovanovic." If I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, I'm hearing "Milovanovic," thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Haynes. We are in agreement here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's Dragomir Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I apologise. Do you know if this had anything to do with the operation you were on in the spring of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that the operations we were launching and that I took part in was the result of this directive, so probably the Main Staff wrote an order to the corps. All I know is that I was there and that Drina Corps conducted those operations, but I don't know that they are the result and consequence of this particular directive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And let's just note, before we leave, that on the top of this, it's from the Main Staff, and its number is 02/5-210, dated 19 November [Realtime transcript read in error "1994"]. That's page 1. Now, if we could go to 65 ter 3029. And similar to what you'd mentioned, here we have a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, there's an error on the page 44, line 8. Instead of the year 1994, it should read "1992."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrusic, that's correct. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, this is -- we're all in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
