utterances.text: Now, as you'd mentioned, here we have a Drina Corps document dated a few days later, the 24th of November. This is to the Zvornik Command, personally to the commander or Chief of Staff. Do you remember who was commander of the Zvornik Brigade in November 24, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I don't mind if you lead on that question. You're cross-examining. You know who it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sometimes I want to hear what the witness says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's continue. Let's not lose precious time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly when General Pandurevic arrived in Zvornik from the Tactical Group Visegrad, but I do know that during that period, Major Obrenovic was certainly down there, because he was there from the start. But I don't know whether this period -- when the corps was being formed, whether General Pandurevic was down there already.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't think he was at that point, but Mr. Haynes gives me more credit than -- I don't remember every detail, but I want to ask you about this. We see that in the top of this, it says: "Pursuant to directive of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska strictly confidential number ...," and I need -- I think you've been alerted to this before, but this is an important mistake. It should be "02/5" in the English, not "3," dated 19 November. So we have a clear reference to directive 4 in this order to the Zvornik Brigade; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The year is 1992 here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry if I said "1994."

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, what you said, well, the directive is mentioned, and it was on the basis of this directive that an order was sent to the Zvornik Brigade, to the attention of the commander, personally, or the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And we see in number 1 that there's some similar language to what I just read to you. It says: "Launch an attack using the main body of troops and major equipment to inflict on the enemy the highest possible losses, exhaust them, break them up, or force them to surrender, and force the Muslim local population to abandon the area of Cerska, Zepa, Srebrenica and Gorazde." So, sir, was this order to the Zvornik Brigade part of the order that you were operating under when you were involved in the Cerska and Konjevic Polje part of the operation you've discussed?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of us who took part in that operation, I mean the officers' cadre and the military section and the units taking part, had before us only a single task, and that was to route of the enemy. What it says here, the Muslim local population forced to abandon the area, et cetera, let me repeat: The Muslim population was never our goal or our decision, those of us who took part in that combat and those operations, and I remember on several occasions the conduct of General Pandurevic specifically towards the civilian population. So nobody gave us that kind of order. Our order was trenches, bunkers, the enemy. And the civilian population on both sides, that is to say, both on the Serb side and on the Muslim side, automatically left the area without any force or military force used against them, but our -- so our goal was just trenches, bunkers, the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So then you would agree with me that as a trained former JNA officer and someone that learned about the Geneva Conventions, this is an illegal order suggesting that the local population be forced to leave?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would use a stronger term, linked to the population, but please believe me, we soldiers, those of us who took part in those combat operations, the population was never our goal, and we always preferred to fight in areas where there was no Muslim population or where there were no civilians at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So you're telling me that you and Vinko Pandurevic disregarded this order, which we now know originated from General Mladic, President Karadzic, General Zivanovic? You guys disregarded these orders from your superiors for this particular operation?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the part of the order that was conveyed to me, or the part of the order conveyed to me with respect to combat, battles, we carried out that order. We didn't disregard it. But nobody conveyed to me ever, nor did I ever hear of what it says here, because I didn't receive these orders myself. The Communications Battalion never received orders of this type, to the effect that the Muslim population was the goal. And I know from experience in all the battle fronts throughout Republika Srpska that the population on both sides even -- well, would abandon the area before the battle started. Before we actually reached the area, they tended to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did the Muslims blow up all the mosques in these areas before they left?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were done -- that was done by some idiots when they had left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go on to another subject. You have testified that you had some kind of a role in the late May/early June operation regarding Zeleni Jadar. Can you just briefly describe what your role was again?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What year are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The one he was talking about, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Drina Corps at that time formed a forward command post at Pribicevac. It wasn't an operation; it was just a military activity which the commander of the corps, General Zivanovic, commanded personally, and he formed the Forward Command Post from the Command of his Corps, and I think that at that Forward Command Post there was Colonel Vicic as an operative, Colonel Veletic, Colonel Vukota, who was there, and that was the composition of the Forward Command Post of the Command. And as an officer from the Communications Battalion, I, on the ground, executed the communications plan for that military activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's it, you were just the coms guy?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in that particular operation I was the coms guy, just like in any of the other operations that we've been discussing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, I know -- I didn't mean to suggest only the coms guys, I shouldn't have said that, but you weren't involved in any leadership role?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's take a look at 65 ter 4097. This is a document by General Zivanovic, dated 29 May 1995. Let me -- I have -- well, I think you can see that okay. If you need a hard copy, let me know. This is a document entitled "Taking Control of the Area of Zeleni Jadar," and it says: "After the UNPROFOR leaves their outpost at Zeleni Jadar, Muslim forces will probably try to place Zeleni Jadar under their control." And then it says: "With the goal of preventing the enemy forces from entering Zeleni Jadar and taking control of the factory compound in Zeleni Jadar and Skelani-Podravanje road, I here by order ..." And so this is assuming, I guess, as we see in this order, assuming UNPROFOR is leaving. So it's not talking about any operation to do with UNPROFOR, but this is the operation to fight the Muslims when they come try to fill the gap. And if we go to page 2 in the English, I mean, you can -- I won't read all the various units, and gathering for the attack, and it's supposed to start on 30 May, and it says: "Engage the following officers from the Drina Corps Command to lead the attack in the area of Zeleni Jadar." And there's "Vicic," and that should be a "Veletic," like you said, and "Major Milenko Jevdjevic." And then, like you said: "I shall personally command the engaged forces from the IKM of the Drina Corps at Pribicevac. The engaged officers from Drina Corps are to be in Skelani by 1400 hours ..." So you're supposed to be in Skelani to lead the attack, and we know from your career that you were a commander in the war and went on to be an even higher commander, so I'm sure you were more than able, in 1995, to lead this. So is this just wrong or does this help you remember you had a bit more of a leadership role than you're telling us now?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think in writing this order, there is a slight imprecision in point 3. It says "for leading the forces in the attack," and then the following officers are named, amongst them myself. And then in the next sentence, the person issuing the order turns this around and said: "I shall personally command the engaged forces from the forward command post of Pribicevac." So that means that the only person who could command those forces and who was in command of the forces at that time at Zeleni Jadar was Corps Commander General Zivanovic, whereas these three persons were his specials from the different fields, the different branches, who should be on hand. And I was on hand to provide secure communication. And later in my career I became a commander, but certainly not then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So he's just flat-out wrong when he says you're to lead the attack? Nobody's suggesting you're in command of the operation?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that it's clear to everyone here that in addition to the corps commander and the general and his three assistants, that I, as the fifth person, I'm fifth in row and the youngest in terms of rank, and the duty of Communications Battalion commander, everybody -- it's clear to everybody that I could have had no command role there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, what's clear to me is the -- General Zivanovic is up in the hills in Pribicevac, a safe distance from that, kind of looking down, and he sent you and two other guys to Skelani. And we know where Skelani is. It's a lot closer to the Muslims forces than where he is, and that -- he didn't send you down there just to do coms work, did he?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as Skelani is concerned, we just met -- we just had a meeting to report to Skelani. Now, Skelani are quite a long distance, much further than Pribicevac and the Muslim forces. Pribicevac was just a few hundred metres away, whereas Skelani was almost 15 or even more kilometres away. So General Zivanovic always liked me to be on hand with him, so at the time I had, well, in quotation marks, the luck of being with him at Pribicevac, and I didn't move away from him during that entire military operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to 65 ter 2894. This is a document you spoke about in your testimony recently. It's dated June 2. It's under the name of General Zivanovic, and I think of this document as the "how to take down a UN OP document," because it gives a very interesting and precise direction to the people on the ground on how to do it. And the first thing I want to ask you about this, and if I can show you the original so you can actually see this, because I seem to recall you had made some comments about this, this was picked out of what is known as the Drina Corps collection, Colonel, a huge collection of documents that we didn't have during the Krstic trial, so you'll be seeing a lot more documents that you didn't see in that trial. So, first of all, it's: "The commander of the Bratunac Brigade shall inform in detail the deputy battalion commander Petrovic ..." Now, that's Sretan Petrovic of the Bratunac Brigade; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was the battalion commander in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then as we go down farther, it says: "He shall establish coded communication with Legenda ..." And that is -- Legenda is Milan Jolovic from the Drina Wolves from the Zvornik Brigade; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so did he - as far as you remember - did Legenda's units take part in this?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was then Colonel Pandurevic down there with him or no?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So Legenda would have been under the command of who during the operation?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think under the direct command of General Zivanovic. I don't know if there was any senior officer in between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So now that you've seen the original, do you have any reason to doubt the authenticity of this order?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And if we go on page 2 of -- I think it's of both languages. After giving a very particular description how to deal with the UNPROFOR, it says" ... disable the APC," excuse me, let me read the whole sentence: "If UNPROFOR soldiers continue to reach out to their weapons in order to use it against Legenda, disable the APC with a hand-held rocket-launcher." And he keeps talking about "this is the moment that UNPROFOR should surrender." And it talks about "call Nikolic." And that, I take it, is Momir Nikolic of the Bratunac Brigade. Right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it could be him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So we can conclude that this order was followed, can't we?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the person who issued the order would probably know that best if he were to carry out an analysis. Last week, I spoke in detail about the events I remember from that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, was it carried out or not?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was, but later on some people were dissatisfied with this because was it enough to secure those factories, because the Muslim side could control the Zeleni Jadar area with firepower. But I remember that the Zeleni Jadar-Jasenova road could be used after this, and that was very important for our units on the ground there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I understand how important that was. And, basically, this is an order to scare the daylights out of UNPROFOR and get them to leave that OP; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, more or less, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you would have had the same problem -- I should say the VRS would have had the same problem with all those OPs ringing Srebrenica a month or so later when it was time to attack the enclave?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This observation post in Zeleni Jadar was special, it was specific. I know that in other places, the army did not have any similar intentions or activities. This observation post was specific, in that it was on no-man's land, and for us to move our positions forward and make it possible to use the road without hindrance and put these industrial plants under our control, we had to move our positions probably to the area of that observation post. The assumption of the person carrying out this activity was probably that UNPROFOR, when they observed the movements of our forces to take up our positions, would probably try to prevent this, and the only way for us to take those points was to put up a show of force by our forces. And from all this, you can see great fear and precise instructions to avoid a conflict at any cost, and that is the main gist of this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Doesn't it say if they don't surrender, if they go for their weapons, you're supposed to shoot a "zolja" at an APC?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does say that here, but I saw this document a few days ago for the first time, so that was the first time I'd seen it. And when I read it, I laughed. Perhaps I shouldn't say that, but I think you laughed too, because it is written in language which is not military, as I understand it. It's written as if it had been written by someone who didn't know much about the war, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, you do recall "zoljas" being fired in this operation, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This very effectively ran off the OP from Echo, didn't it, from this OP that we're talking about? They ran off? It's a simple question. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I learned was that in that activity, not a single bullet was fired. It was very quiet. I remember that operation by this, because it was the only operation I'd ever participated in where I knew that not a single bullet had been fired. And it's quite logical that the UNPROFOR OP was scared and they moved their position 200 metres back. That appears quite logical to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It was. I agree with you, this was all very logical, and they had the same problem a month later. And perhaps you'll agree with me that many of the OPs in this area during the attack on Srebrenica, the UN forces fled as well. Some actually came to the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You should have seen the enthusiasm of those UNPROFOR soldiers when they came to our side and their frightened faces when a colleague of theirs, a soldier, was killed by Muslim fire an hour before I encountered them, and that fire was intentional. It was not accidental. That's what I know. Had they seen us as a threat, they would have withdrawn to their bases in Potocari and Srebrenica, because they didn't have to cross anyone's trenches there. They would simply have to withdraw, go back. But they came to our rear, that is, seeking our protection, crossing trenches and passing by gun barrels in the process.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, I won't go over with you the evidence this Court has heard about the attack on the OPs during the assault on Srebrenica. I won't go over the evidence with you about the fact that many of those UN forces were held against their will at the Hotel Fontana and used as hostages and were threatened with death, so I don't think there's a point in that. But let's go over -- unless you'd like to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I believe you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's go to 5D1083. This is a document you saw yesterday, and let me give you the original of this, because you seem to have some kind of problem with this document as well. According to this document, it's -- as you recall, it's in your name. It's a teletype, so there's no signature on it, so that's a mistake in translation. And the English translation is also wrong. There's no mention of the Main Staff. It's the Drina Corps. And it begins -- I won't go through everything, but it says: "After a successful operation and the forceful expulsion of UNPROFOR from the Zeleni Jadar post, the enemy was observed systematically building up large forces and moving them from Srebrenica sector towards the general sector of Zeleni Jadar. Their formation included two OT and one tank." An OT is thought to be an armoured personnel carrier. It goes on, says some other things, and then it says: "The Inhabitants of Zeleni Jadar moved out in panic following UNPROFOR's withdrawal ..." And then when you get to paragraph 2, it starts out with: "In a very precise and professional operation, our firm and daring approach forced the UNPROFOR check-point in Zeleni Jadar to withdraw in panic to Srebrenica." And then it says: "Force was used, but there were no injuries to the UN personnel." And then in number 3, it says: "We have expended small amounts of ammunition and three zoljas." So -- and this is under your name. You've seen the original now. Do you, sir, doubt the authenticity of this document?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here, where the signature is, that this regular combat report was sent to the Command of the Drina Corps from the Pribicevac Forward Command Post on that date, the 3rd of June, and that it was received there at 1900 hours. It was sent to the Chief of Staff, personally. Last week, I said, when the Defence was putting questions to me about this, that I have nothing special to add to all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you don't doubt the authenticity of the document?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to repeat what I said last week. In my view -- well, when I read this document, and knowing what the situation was like to the best of my recollection, I saw that the document does not reflect the actual situation. It's been embellished for whoever was reading it. I certainly did not compile the document. I was the communications man. It was very unusual that in a small operation in which not a single bullet was fired and in which only two companies advanced for a few hundred metres, and which was commanded by the corps commander personally and three colonels, it would be highly unusual for a communications man, who had not moved anywhere from the Pribicevac Forward Command Post, and who had not personally seen what was going on in Zeleni Jadar, to write all this. What I can assume is the following: When I saw this document a few days ago, I was very surprised to see my name down there. I wish I could see the original telegram. If I saw my own signature, that might be clearer. But when this telegram was received at 9.30 in the evening at the -- at Vlasenica, Vesna Bajnic [phoen], my cryptographer, signed her name here. I was already in the corps at that time. I assume this might have been written by Colonel Vukota who was up there then. Zivanovic would be back at the Corps Command, I assume, because I was always went with him when that operation was ongoing, so there's no logic to my having compiled and signed this document and sent it to the Chief of Staff personally, of all people. Well, that's all I can say about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, are you doubting the authenticity of the document?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was compiled by someone who put my name to it. That personal probably had a reason, but I don't want to speculate about it. I don't doubt the authenticity of the document, because it did arrive in the Corps Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This Court and everyone knows that many of the daily combat reports from operations don't get drafted or written by the commander. The commander or the person designated to sending out the report, be they a leader, be they a coms man, be they a senior officer, we know many times will be relying on people that provides information, so isn't that what happened? Someone gave you this information. It went out under your name. You're responsible for that information; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I neither saw this information, nor did I compile it, nor did I take any part in its drafting. It doesn't reflect the actual situation that happened there. You certainly know from the statements by UNPROFOR that three "zoljas" were not fired at them then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We'll get into that in a minute, but I am going to agree with you that there's some embellishment going on here, because we've never seen a tank or two APCs in the hands of the Muslims, either, at that point. But we know that soldiers sometime embellish these things. Okay, let's -- you've invited me to the record of UNPROFOR, and an officer in charge at the time, Major Franken, has testified, and let me go over what he said to you in this courtroom, page 2452, on October 16th, 2006: "We got a report through Bravo Company, the company that was responsible for the area, that there was some movement in front of OP Echo. The movement proved to be Serb infantry. Then the Serb infantry yelled, used a loudspeaker, to tell the OP that they had to go. They had to withdraw, because the Serbs wanted to come in. B Company asked me permission to do that. I denied that. And then they came under attack, and in the end the Serbs took Echo over and the crew withdrew in the very last moment with my authorisation." And then the question was asked: "And when you mention an attack, what did the attack on the OP consist of, sir?" Answer: "There was about 40 infantry supported by a tank and Tango 5 fighters, the main battle tank and a gun on the edge, the ridge at Zeleni Jadar." "And were there shots actually fired during the attack, sir?" "Yes, absolutely. Yes, yes." "And, what, was there damage to the OP?" "Well, the tower was hit, the observation tower was hit by firing -- the firing main battle tank, and the area was fired at by the gun. It was an anti-aircraft gun standing up there but was used to support the Serb attack." Now, from Mr. Franken's account and from the accounts we've heard, perhaps the cloud of war gets mixed up between a "zolja," a tank, some kind of a Praga, but clearly, sir, does this help refresh your recollection? There were shots fired at this OP, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A "zolja" and a tank are two very different weapons. When a tank fires, there's thunder on all sides. So this person would probably have written that a tank was used and that tank ammunition was fired, but he only said three "zoljas." To use a "zolja," you have to shoot it from a distance of about 100 metres in order to hit an APC precisely, so that you can see that the testimony of that major and this statement are very different. In any case, he, as a soldier, would have to give some arguments as to why he withdrew from a position he was supposed to keep, so I understand him. I know why he had to embellish his report, too. But the two reports are different.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I think we can agree that both you and Major Franken are receiving information from those that are being fired at, and I think we can leave it at that, unless you want to make any further comment. Okay, something you said in your direct I've got to ask you about. Page 29490, you were asked by counsel, I believe it was -- well, I don't remember who it was. It was one of the Defence counsel: "Do you know whether the Drina Corps forces had sniper weapons in its armoury?" And you answered: "I often toured the front-lines in the Drina Corps area of responsibility, and believe me when I say that I never saw a single soldier who was issued with a sniper rifle. I like weapons, and that's why I know. Semi-automatic sniper rifles have only ten bullets. You can only fire single shots. And you can talk to any soldier and ask them, and they will tell you that they preferred to have automatic weapons issued to them, and we didn't have such rifles at all in our stocks. Well, there were situations where shots were fired from light machine-guns or semi-automatic rifles, and then when it buzzes past somebody's head, the person assumes he was targeted by a sniper. I know that such assumptions were made on our side, and probably it was done on the other side too." The sniper rifles used by the VRS had a very particular calibre shell, didn't it? Can you tell us what it was?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The weapons I learned about in the army include a 7.9-millimetre sniper rifle. I'm not sure what year that model came out, and that sniper weapon was issued only to some special units or sabotage platoons, and then only when they were on a special task. The units holding the front around both enclaves, and our units participating in combat where I was, never, in all the four years of the war, had, as far as I was able to see, a soldier issued with a sniper rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to 65 ter 4108. I'll try not to spend too much time here. But, sir, as that's coming up, you'll see that it's a 27 April 1994 report from the 8th Srebrenica Operations Group Command, and it's an intelligence report. And it says on this second sentence on 26th of April, 1994: "An aggressor sniper aiming from the area of Pajici at the demilitarised zone severely wounded a 17-year-old boy." You didn't get reports like that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a report which is part of the correspondence between the BH army or, rather, its units. We did not get these reports. It's a report from the then 8th Operations Group of Srebrenica, which they were sending to the Command of the 2nd Corps in Tuzla; that is, the army in Srebrenica was informing its corps in Tuzla about something that happened on that day and about a boy who was hit by a bullet and who was severely wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I apologise. My question was imprecise. I didn't think, unless you intercepted this, that you would have received it, but would you have -- wouldn't you have known that forces were, you know, sniping at civilians in Srebrenica on this period?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and we couldn't have intercepted this conversation either - you asked me that - because at that time the 28th Division in Srebrenica already had devices for compressed and secret transmission. This was transported by UNPROFOR or some other civilian organisation bringing in supplies to Srebrenica, and in that period it was already very difficult for us to intercept their communications because they had devices for compressed transmission and we were unable to goniometer that and listen in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I've got two more similar documents to show you. 4D00134, this is the same kind of a thing. It's a Muslim report from the 28th Division to their Command in 2nd Corps, and there's just another report here, that on June 10th, 1995, it says -- I think the third paragraph down, but I don't think it really important to actually read it. But it's on 10 June 1995, "The enemy wounded a civilian from a sniper rifle in D. Polje, the area of responsibility of the 280th Brigade." And then if we go to 65 ter 4109, another report 3 July 1995, this is another intelligence report getting closer to our time, we see on the topic: "The Aggressor." "Chetniks are still carrying out reconnaissance in force of our forward defence lines and shooting fiercely with infantry and anti-aircraft weapons at all defence lines of the 28th Ground Army Division and civilian facilities. Particularly fierce sniper fire is coming from the direction of Buljim, trig point 820, Zeleni Jadar and Zaledje area, where a woman was killed by sniper fire yesterday." So the 3rd of July, I guess that's right before you got to Pribicevac, so perhaps you didn't hear about this, that you were -- that the VRS is allegedly engaged in serious sniper fire as a prelude to the major attack. So did you know, right before you got there, that there was sniper fire going on into the enclave, early July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and I've already told you about that. A good sniper with an ordinary rifle can hit a target at 700 to 800 metres; a marksman, I'm sorry. Now, I don't contest the facts of this report, but what I'm saying is that this did not happen with a sniper weapon, because we didn't have any, or very few of them, and I've talked about that, just as I claim that our side, in some of our reports, would say that the enemy used sniper fire to attack us, although we officers knew that the enemy didn't have sniper rifles either. But as soon as it was an individual shot, then everybody automatically concluded that it was sniper fire, and if there was a burst of gunfire, then it would be assumed that this was from a rifle. But there are rifles that can shoot single bullets, too, without it being called "sniper fire." I discussed this and talked about it, and I stand by what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to 65 ter 4094. I'm going to go over a few more documents, and maybe you might agree with me that you made a mistake on this point. But let's see what I can show you. What we found is a programme for a sniper course for the VRS for 1995, and it came out of the -- the first page, you can see, is entitled "The Republika Srpska Army, Main Staff." I'm not going to go through all of it. It's basically an outline for the -- I think for the corps, on how to set up a good sniper training course. And were you aware that they had plans for sniper training in 1995 from the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime towards the end of the war in the Drinjaca Training Centre or Kozluk, it says "Drinjaca" here, but anyway that was -- well, could I look at the whole document, please? Maybe I would be able to comment on it better then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just -- you can flip through it and ignore -- there is some highlighted stuff. I don't remember why I did that, but ... And perhaps you can flip through it slowly so people can see what the witness is seeing; just the rough outline of a course, basically instructions on how to run such a course. I really don't have any other questions about this, just about your general knowledge of whether there was such a course.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you happen to have here what period of time this was in 1995, because this is just a programme for a sniper course of the VRS which somebody compiled as a document, set it down on paper. It doesn't actually deal with the execution of it, how many participants, where and when. This is just a theoretical programme compiled at some time in 1995. It's not clear when. The war was over in 1995. But, anyway, it was derived from the Main Staff. Now, by the time it went down to the corps and the corps devised their own plan, that would make it 1996. So do you have anything more precise, because there's no date on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, that's why I asked you the question. Do you remember a sniper course?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what you gave me here, this does not deal at all with any sniper courses. Had they been put into practice, had they been held in some relevant time of 1995, it doesn't say that. This is just a programme which the Main Staff devised --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I understand that. That's why I'm asking you. You were into weapons and sniper stuff. Do you remember did the Drina Corps develop a sniper course? It's a simple question, because I agree with you, it's just the Main Staff layout on how to conduct -- you know, we had how to conduct the takedown of the UN, and now we have how to conduct a sniper course.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At the beginning of 1996, I was already the brigade commander in Sehovici, which is possibly when this plan/programme should have been elaborated further down at the level of the Drina Corps, and I don't remember I sent any of my soldiers for sniper training, and certainly it didn't come into effect in 1995, which means it didn't earlier on either. So my answer to that question is "no."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And this came out of the Main Staff. This is a training document, isn't it? This would have come out under the Administration for Operations and Training?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they would deal with training.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who was the man in charge of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Prosecutor tell us the time period for this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The front page, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think the witness, himself, looks at this document on the basis that it was formulated possibly in 1995, and then he did mention its possible implementation in 1996, because it couldn't have been earlier. That's how I understood the witness earlier on. I mean, if the witness wishes to correct me or correct even Mr. McCloskey, he's free to do so, but I see him nodding. Yes, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we're dealing with 1996, then how is it relevant?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can perhaps -- either you deal with this, if you wish, or else, Mr. Petrusic, on re-examination you can cover this. But the witness, I think, explained where 1996 would fit in, because according to him there was no way it could have been implemented in 1995, although it could have been drawn up in 1995. But, anyway, I mean, I don't want to waste time on this. Please, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So, sir, who was the man in charge of the Main Staff Administration for Operations and Training, the chief of the Operations and Training Administration of the Main Staff in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, because the formation of the Main Staff differed from the formation and establishment of the corps and brigades. All I know is that some people who worked -- I know some people who worked there. Now, whether they were sectors or departments or what, anyway, corps establishment differs from staff establishment, so I don't have that information to hand just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could it have been General Miletic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to those operative matters, I know that in that administration, or department, or sector, whatever it was called - I don't know the exact title - there was General Obradovic, General Miletic, Trkulja, and perhaps some five or six other officers who dealt with that area of activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, in the corps and in the brigade, the branch is called "Operations and Training." It's always under the Chief of Staff. It has a boss. In this case, it was General Miletic. You know that; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was sectors up there at the Main Staff. We say "up there" because it was Han Pijesak. There were sectors up there. Now, who occupied what duties and posts within the sectors, I really can't say, I don't know, because I went to the Main Staff on rare occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go on. Let's look at 65 ter number 230. This is a document that the Court has seen. It's been around for a while. Let me give you the whole thing, and hand me back that other stuff so we don't get all mixed up. Now, this is a report that all the brigades had to send up to the corps. This is particularly from the Bratunac Brigade, and it's for the first half of 1995, basically 1 January through June 30, 1995. And it talks about a lot of things, but let me go through it chronologically and get your comments. Page 9 of the English, it should be page 27 in your issue, and this is entitled "Inventory of Ammunition and Ordnance on 30 June 1995." Have you got to page 27? There's a --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So in this inventory, we go down to number 8, and it says: "Bullet, 7.9 millimetre for sniper." And the Serbian uses basically the same word. It just spells it properly, S-N-A-J-P-E-R. So if they don't have any sniper rifles, what are they doing with 1.350 sniper bullets in their inventory?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they have it in the inventory in the depot, the warehouse. You see that this is the warehouse, the depot. They're not up at their combat position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the next page. This is entitled: "Inventory of Ammunition and Ordnance Received in the Warehouse." It's page 25 on yours.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I'm saying. That's what I've just been saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So here's -- number 6 is 1.905 pieces in the warehouse. Then we go down: "Issued from the warehouse." Now, "Issued from the warehouse," sort of speaks for itself. Who's the warehouse issuing this ammunition to?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't say who it was issued to and when it was issued, for what requirements, to what unit and so on. This is some internal record, and I assume that the assistant commander for the rear of the Bratunac Brigade compiled this, because this was an opportunity for him, in a six-month period, to make his own records and to have a review and inventory. And probably for the people in the warehouse, they provided him with the information of what the stock was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, can a 7.9 millimetre sniper bullet be used in another weapon?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Which one?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The M-48 rifle. It's the same calibre, 7.9.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know what happens to the gun when you shoot a sniper bullet in it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we used that -- the people in charge of warehouses used rifles like that, for example, the security for warehouses, and we tried to have the automatic weapons up at the combat positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: One more question --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The security guards used that kind of rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... and we'll be done, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, same thing, but let's go to, let's see page 13 in the B/C/S, 19 in the English, and this is the section on training. And it's annex number 1, and it says: "Realisation of training and participation in courses during the first half of 1995." Number 7: "Sniper training. Place, Bratunac and Bjelovar. Number of candidates, 13. Number of days, seven. Remarks, accomplished." So in the first half of 1995, Blagojevic is reporting to the Drina Corps that 13 of his guys have taken a seven-day course in sniper training and have accomplished that course; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly, if he wrote that there, although, quite sincerely, I have experience with this -- these analyses of combat readiness. I wrote things like that myself. And during the war they were a big problem, because you had to find the time to write all this down, have all these papers and documents, whereas you were facing a difficult situation, so you gave an operative the task of doing this and seeing that everything was in order and to satisfy the form. So possibly he might have conducted some sort of course, but this does not mean he had any weapons or anything like that, semi-automatic rifles, and that they were distributed up at the positions around the enclaves, and that they fired from those positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Maybe we better take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We'll have a 25-minute break. That means that we'll resume at 1.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, thank you, Mr. President. Could we go to 65 ter number 4091.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Colonel, we've -- you've been explaining about the bullets. You're explaining about the courses. Now let me show you a 1994 document from the Bratunac Brigade, dated 10 July, and it's entitled "Status of Sniper Rifles, Silencers, Reconnaissance, Radars, and Infrared Binoculars." And you'll see, as you look at it under Roman numeral II: "Sniper rifle, 7.9-millimetre, PAP." And it lists a bunch of people; 17, as a matter of fact. And this is a listing of the people who have been assigned sniper rifles, isn't it, some with scopes, some without scopes?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is a review. I read through it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So now we have some 17 men who have been issued these sniper rifles, and we've seen all the bullets, we've seen the training. Are you ready to agree with me now that Bratunac Brigade had sniper rifles, bullets to fire them, and received training by July 1995 on how to use them?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are slight imprecisions. For example, 6, it says in the warehouse, two pieces. Now -- of the 1st Infantry Battalion warehouse, that is. So these aren't all the names of the people individually. And number 18, for example, says "Warehouse," too. So I stand by what I said; that in those areas, and we're talking about the Srebrenica enclave, I never saw soldiers being issued sniper rifles or having snipers among their weapons. And specifically here you can see that you have snipers in warehouses according to battalions. Had the goal been to effect sniper fire, they would have issued the soldiers with the snipers from the warehouse. Now, if we talk about the Sarajevo battle front, where the lines were less than 100 metres apart, I would agree with your thesis. But, however, in Srebrenica, where the trenches were several hundred metres apart and where the population lived behind those trenches on both sides, then that weaponry would not have had any sense or effect, because they were large distances that would have to have been targeted. So I never saw anybody hold a sniper over there, and that's what I said before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to 65 ter 4093. This is an 18 June 1995 report from the Command of the Bratunac Brigade, in the name of its commander, Blagojevic. It's a regular combat report. Under "Logistical Supply," you'll see in 5 that under "Expenditure," 150 bullets had been expended, sniper bullets. So despite everything you've seen in the records, you're still suggesting they're not firing sniper shells?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps it would be a good idea to take a look at the course organised by the Bratunac Brigade, if it was indeed organised and implemented, and then to see whether, for their purposes, these 150 bullets might have been used, because I really wouldn't like to speculate. It does, indeed, say here that expenditure was 150 pieces. Now, whether that was expenditure on that particular day, that seems to me to be unbelievable, because if you find two more reports like that over four years, that sniper bullets to this number were used, I personally don't believe that. And if 150 bullets could have been fired on that day, then there must have been shooting every day. So I don't want to speculate whether the expenditure was for that, or for the course, or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, let's not speculate what those 17 guys -- how many shots they were firing. Let's hope that was training. But let's go to 65 ter 4098, an 8 July report from the Drina Corps, Lazar Ocamovic [phoen]. It's to the Main Staff and the rear command post and the technical department: "We're sending you the report on the consumption of ammunition and explosives for 1 June through 30 June." So we've got one month for the Drina Corps, 7.9 millimetre for sniper, 1.825. That's consumed, that's fired, that's shot. Are you telling us right now that you still don't believe any Drina Corps units fired any shots at the enclaves?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I claimed from the very beginning that I never saw any of the units who held the front towards the enclaves, that their soldiers at those positions had any snipers, any sniper rifles. That's what I said, and I explained that and said that from the tactics of using that kind of weaponry, it was a very great distance to the target and a sniper would not be effective as it would have been in the Sarajevo area. Now, in this same report under "1," you have that 25 pieces are pistol ammunition, 7.65 millimetres, the small pistols were used, and 7.62 millimetres, also a pistol bullet, 3.830 pieces. Now, I can place a bet that on that day never -- nobody ever shot from either that pistol or that other weapon, but that that person in the rear wanted to tell the person in logistics in the Main Staff to draw their attention to what ammunitions they needed in the warehouse that they lacked. So this largely refers to all the rest of the ammunition that was needed, the supplies of which were needed, and so on. So my knowledge is this: To say that I didn't see any snipers over there, I didn't see any soldiers being issued snipers, and I explained that as far as I was concerned, it was logical that that should be the case or should not be the case, because weapons of that kind would not have proved effective, given the distance of the target.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, I'm sure you recall testifying that you said that the Drina Corps didn't even have such weapons in their stocks, so I don't want to argue with you about it, but let's go to the last document on this one, 65 ter 4099. Do you wish to withdraw your statement under oath that the Drina Corps did not have any sniper rifles in their stocks?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you quote this to me from the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I could, but I'm not going to, because I don't know where it is. I'm sorry. But you, I'm sure, remember it.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly didn't say they did not have this. I said I did not see the units around the enclave that the soldiers who were there had sniper weapons. I simply did not see that any of the soldiers there were issued with such weapons, whether the Drina Corps had such weapons in the depots and whether it actually issued those weapons to someone, I don't know. I didn't see. I was concentrating only on the units around the enclave, focusing on what I, myself, saw during my frequent visits there, my frequent sojourns there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Page 29491, "Semi-automatic sniper rifles have only ten bullets. You can only fire single shots, and you can talk to any soldier and ask them, and they will tell you that they prefer to have automatic weapons issued to them, and we didn't have such rifles at all in our stocks." My question is: Do you wish to withdraw that statement now that I've shown you these documents and we've seen these sniper rifles?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I abide by that, because the units manning the positions did not have such weapons, such rifles. That I saw with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, we can look at 65 ter 4099. This is the Milici Brigade. According to this, on November 12 they had 17 sniper rifles. They were also around the enclave. Do you want to go to the Skelani Battalion as well? We don't have time and I'm not going to go there, but do you want to change what you've said?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't want to change what I've said, but I ask you for a little patience. I have to see the document in its entirety to see what it is, actually. I don't see the end of this document. This is simply a list of all the weapons of the Milici Brigade, but where each particular weapon was, that's a different question. This is an inventory of all the weapons they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I think we can go on to another topic. You talked a bit about the Krivaja 95 attack plan and its objectives, and will you agree with me that one of the objectives of the attack of Krivaja 95 was to create conditions for the elimination of the enclaves, Srebrenica in particular?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I knew personally, without looking at any documents, because I didn't receive any such documents, I only received communications documents, those were the only documents available to me in the relevant period, is that the units of the Drina Corps had the task of sealing off the enclave and prevent communication between the two enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa, and also prevent incursions from those enclaves into the depth of our territory, as well as communications between their small armed groups with Tuzla, Olovo, and Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was one of the objectives to create the conditions for the elimination of the enclaves, Srebrenica in particular?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know it now?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The actual situation developed in such a way that the Muslim units in those two enclaves suffered the military defeat, after which there was deportation of the population and the other things that were done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I understand that, but that doesn't come close to answering my question. Do you know now, from any source, that one of the objectives of the Krivaja 95 plan was to create conditions for the elimination of the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have had occasion here to read some documents which contain that phrase or sentence, "to create the conditions for the elimination of the enclave," but in the relevant period, until I saw those documents, I did not know of the existence of that sentence there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And we can all agree that this was on the Krivaja 95 plan 65 ter 107, page 3 in the English, under "Objective," page 2 in B/C/S, and so I think we can save a little time on that. Now, you've testified that you packed up the coms van at the Forward Command Post in the early evening hours of 11 July. I think you made that very clear. It's the position of the Prosecutor now, as it was when Mr. Harmon cross-examined you, as I'm sure you remember many years ago, that that's wrong; that the coms van and people left on the afternoon of 12 July. And you've also testified that you had a meeting -- or that you were at the meeting where Mladic said that you would go to Zepa with Vinko Pandurevic, Krstic and others. It's the position of the Prosecution that you are wrong on that point; that that meeting did, in fact, occur, and it happened on the 12th of July, that you were in Bratunac on the 12th of July. Now, you've also testified previously that when you testified for General Krstic, that you felt General Krstic became commander after he came back from the party at the Jela Restaurant. Now, it's the position of the Prosecution, and I don't think it's contested at this trial, that General Krstic became commander of the Drina Corps in a small ceremony informally held in Vlasenica at the Command, with several people, where General Mladic announced to the Drina Corps that Zivanovic was leaving and General Krstic was to become the commander. This was a significant issue at the Krstic trial, and it's our position that he became commander on the 13th of July at that meeting. Now, sir, let's go over some of the documents. I'm sure you'll recall some of the documents that Mr. Harmon --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I have a little time to respond to these three accusations by the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As much as you like, Mr. Jevdjevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want to deal with three statements put forward by the Prosecutor, analysing what I stated in relation to what the Prosecutor is staying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so you know, Colonel, many of the documents that you've discussed when you testified previously, I will have for you to see, so you'll be able to talk about them, as well as your initial comments to me. I meant that to you to let you know where I was going with the documents and what our position was. But you're of course always able to respond to my statements that I'm required to give to you.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will avail myself of His Honour's leave to respond. First, it is not clear to me by any means that in the statement that I gave in April 2000 to your investigator in Banja Luka, under some highly irregular circumstances, up to my testimony in 2001 before this Tribunal, as well as my testimony last week, how anyone can say that I, with my soldiers and equipment, did not leave Pribicevac on the 11th, that I didn't go along the way I said I had gone along, and that I did not see what I saw, and that I did not attend the meeting in the evening in the Command of the Bratunac Brigade on that day, the 11th. Some things I said before this Court that I remember or that I assume, but the things I have just mentioned are things I know and remember very well. I remember my departure from the Forward Command Post on the 11th, when it ceased to exist because the communications centre there ceased to exist, and the meeting held by General Mladic on the evening of the 11th in the barracks of the Bratunac Brigade, exactly as I testified, and I fail to comprehend how, after so many years of dealing with this topic, someone can still maintain that this was not the case. As regards the hand-over of duty between General Krstic and General Zivanovic. On the 12th, I went to the Zepa Forward Command Post. There was a meeting there in the evening of the 13th, when General Mladic lined up a few men, as you said, and conveyed to them information that General Krstic would be the new corps commander and Colonel Andric the new Chief of Staff. I was already at the Zepa Forward Command Post at that time, and I did not have this information. I received this information secondhand. Someone simply told me about this, as a soldier -- and also I did not have occasion to see the documents I have seen here over the past few days, informing the units of this hand-over. As a soldier, I failed to comprehend how, on the 13th of July, when the Drina Corps was probably carrying out the most unusual combat activities in the course of its entire existence, someone could replace the corps commander not as punishment and not as a promotion, because it was quite logical that while the Stupcanica operation was ongoing and there was major fighting with an enemy column breaking through from Srebrenica, it would be quite logical for the corps commander to sit in Vlasenica and coordinate these two extremely difficult operations. It is highly illogical that General Krstic, the corps commander, and his Chief of Staff, Colonel Andric, should in this period be at Zepa, that Andric should be leading his hundred men as Chief of Staff, and respond out of breath on the communications line when Colonel Trivic was wounded, and so on and so forth. During this trial, I have had occasion to see certain documents which show beyond doubt that there actually was a hand-over of duty at that time. But as it is a rule in the army that when a decree from the president of the republic arrives about the hand-over of duties in the corps, the Main Staff writes an order and sets a seven day time period for the hand-over to be carried out. After that, a record has to be made of that hand-over of duty, and based on that record and that date, all the legal matters and all the powers and entitlements and benefits of the corps commander start running. So this is how I'm interpreting that situation. Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, there's one more point that I should give you a chance. You'll probably want to explain as well. It's the Prosecution position that you could not have travelled through Potocari from Srebrenica on the evening of 11th of July freely, because you would have had to pass through a Dutch barricade, through thousands of Muslims who would have been quite upset at that point, as they were the next day when the Serbs arrived. So that's another point that is part of the Prosecution's case that we differ with you on.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every UNPROFOR barricade and all their duties in that connection ceased on the 10th and the 11th. I passed through Potocari along the only road leading from Srebrenica towards Bratunac, and that was my assessment of the situation. Last Sunday -- last week, that is, I won't repeat myself, I said I saw several thousand civilians, that UNPROFOR was concentrated in small groups among the civilians, but for the most part in their base. And to avoid repeating what I've already said, I abide by every word I said in this connection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's go through some of the documents on these topics, and you can hear my questions and you'll be able to give your responses. And I'll try to be brief, and if you can try to be brief and to the point, I think it will be clearer for everyone. Can you tell me, because I think you changed slightly in your testimony, what time do you think you actually left Pribicevac with the van, the coms van?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by saying that I slightly changed my testimony. I think you should explain to me, because I don't want to prejudge anything you may have in mind. As regards the communications centre at Pribicevac, I packed up before nightfall, at around 1900 hours, and set out towards Bratunac. And I stated that to your investigator eight years ago in Banja Luka. He tried to persuade me for an hour that that had not been the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So just so it's clear, what time did you actually start driving out of Pribicevac? I understood you packed up at 1900 hours, but what time did you actually start leaving, roughly, as close as you can get?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around that time. I can't be precise, but I know that I passed through Potocari just as it was getting dark, at dusk, twilight. That's sometime between 8.30 to 8.45 or 9.00 p.m. So I needed about an hour from Pribicevac to Potocari. Calculating back, it would have been a quarter past 8.00 or 8.30, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how many vehicles went with you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was just my vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you describe that vehicle?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The vehicle we used is a TAM 110. That's the Marljiboro [phoen] TAM Mobil Factory. It's a truck, and it had a container on it, according to establishment, and in that container we had the equipment indispensable for communications. And two or three of my men were in that cabin in the back, and I was in front, sitting next to the driver. Next to me was in a place where there is no seat, but only the hood of the motor, my sergeant was sitting there. He was sitting between the driver and me. And I know the names of the drivers and the sergeant, and we used that vehicle to go from Pribicevac when we had packed up all the equipment and all the aerials into that vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how many men from your unit did you have with you at Pribicevac that last day?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a small communications unit, between four and six men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell me the names of the men you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Momir Bakmas [phoen]; he was my sergeant. He's still in the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Veljko Vukosaljevic [phoen], the driver; Selso Kolovic [phoen] or Sokolac; Mirko Pakalovic [phoen], from the village of Sekotin [phoen], Vlasenica; Oliver Sekulic from Sokolac, he was the cryptographer. And along with those four, I think that squad included two other soldiers from my Communications Battalion, but I don't remember their names. But those four almost always went with me everywhere, and that's why I remember them very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did all those people that you just named leave with you the evening of the 11th or did some remain behind?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one stayed behind at Pribicevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So they all fit in this big vehicle and the container or did they have another vehicle?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't have any other vehicles. We all used that vehicle. The only thing I don't remember well, I think one or two of them were natives of Bratunac, and I don't know whether they stayed behind that evening to visit their parents. But we all used that vehicle. That was the only vehicle with which we participated in the Srebrenica operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you leave a teletype machine back there or any radio equipment to receive messages?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. At Pribicevac, there had been, since 1994, at the disposal of Colonel Vukota, a teleprinter and an encryption device, but we who arrived from Vlasenica packed up what we had brought with us, and we left the Forward Command Post on the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did Mr. Sekulic go with you; you're sure?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And about what time did you get to the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I arrived at the Bratunac Brigade, and it was already completely dark. I think it was probably after 9.00 p.m. It was sometime between 9.00 and 9.30. Perhaps a quarter past 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what time was it when you first saw General Krstic or General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw General Krstic before the meeting started. I first saw my communications man who was in a jeep, constantly accompanying General Krstic, and he was carrying General Krstic's mobile communications device towards -- used to communicate with the units participating in the Krivaja operation. I asked him whether he had had any problems, whether General Krstic had asked about me and so on. And as there hadn't been any problems, I probably met General Krstic between 9.30 and 10.00, according to my rough estimation, simply to tell him that I had packed up the communications equipment and that I and my signalsmen were now in the compound of the Bratunac barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when did you first see Mladic when you got back -- or when you got, excuse me, to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw General Mladic for the first time when the meeting started in the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: About what time was that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my estimation, that meeting had to begin at around 2200 hours, around 2200 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, it's the position of the Prosecutor that on the evening of the 11th of July, the VRS was not really sure where the Muslim 28th Division was. They could have been heading en masse towards Zepa. They could have been going towards Tuzla. They could have been up in the hills. Can you tell us, sir - just one last question - how was it that with that being the situation and the backdrop, you were able to pick up the coms people and van and leave without any orders to do so, as you've testified?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had information that already on the 10th of July, after our counter-attack and retaking of the Zivkovo Brdo elevation, every organised resistance of the enemy had ceased. And on the 11th, after the bombing, we had precise information that the 28th Division was grouping in the northwestern part of the enclave; that is, the area between Srebrenica and Konjevic Polje and Kasaba, and that there were indications that a smaller part had the intention of breaking through towards Zepa. This was information we had from intelligence listening in to the communications of the 28th Division, because at the Pribicevac Forward Command Post we had a squad from the 4th Radio Reconnaissance Platoon of the Drina Corps listening in to the communications of the 28th Division. When you are dealing with communications, at any point you can evaluate up to where the units have reached and how the combat disposition is moving forward, how it's advancing. Command posts move forward in leaps and bounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We have to quit now, because if we don't leave now, the next trial will be delayed. So you'll be able to finish that question and add anything you need to it, so we'll start again. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Thank you, Mr. Jevdjevic. We'll continue tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
